content: Early pregnancy factor (EPF), also known as early conception factor (ECF), is a protein associated with mammalian embryos shortly after fertilization. It may consist of more than one molecule and was first described in 1976. EPF is detected using the rosette inhibition test. It is present in maternal serum (blood plasma) shortly after fertilization and can also be found in cervical mucus and amniotic fluid. In sheep, EPF can be detected within 72 hours of mating, in mice within 24 hours, and in the media surrounding human embryos fertilized in vitro within 48 hours of fertilization. However, some studies have failed to replicate the detection of EPF in in vitro embryos. EPF has been detected as early as six hours after mating. The rosette inhibition test for EPF is indirect, and substances with similar effects may interfere with the test. For example, pig semen has been shown to inhibit rosette formation, leading to a positive test result for one day in sows mated with a vasectomized boar, but not in sows stimulated without semen exposure. Several studies following the discovery of EPF were unable to consistently detect it in post-conception females, raising questions about the validity of the original experiments. However, progress in characterizing EPF has been made, and its existence is now widely accepted in the scientific community. Early embryos are not believed to directly produce EPF. Instead, they are thought to produce another chemical that induces the maternal system to create EPF. After implantation, EPF may be produced directly by the conceptus. EPF functions as an immunosuppressant and, along with other substances associated with early embryos, is believed to help prevent the maternal immune system from attacking the embryo. Injecting anti-EPF antibodies into mice after mating significantly reduced the number of successful pregnancies and pups, but no effect on growth was observed when mouse embryos were cultured in media containing anti-EPF antibodies. While some actions of EPF, such as rosette inhibition, are consistent across mammals, other immunosuppressant mechanisms vary between species. In mice, EPF levels are high during early pregnancy but decline to non-pregnant levels by day 15. In humans, EPF levels remain high for the first 20 weeks of pregnancy, then decline and become undetectable within eight weeks after delivery. Recent research suggests that EPF may also be associated with cell proliferation in various biological contexts, not just embryonic development. In 1979, it was proposed that EPF could serve as a marker for very early pregnancy testing and as a means to monitor the viability of ongoing pregnancies in livestock. Interest in EPF for this purpose has persisted, although current testing methods have not proven sufficiently accurate for livestock management. In humans, modern pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), which is not present until after implantation, occurring six to twelve days after fertilization. In contrast, EPF is present within hours of fertilization. While other pre-implantation signals have been identified, EPF is believed to be the earliest possible marker of pregnancy. Several studies have found EPF to be highly accurate as a pregnancy test in humans. EPF may also be used to determine whether the pregnancy prevention mechanisms of birth control methods act before or after fertilization. A study evaluating EPF levels in women with intrauterine devices (IUDs) concluded that post-fertilization mechanisms significantly contribute to the effectiveness of these devices. For groups that define pregnancy as beginning with fertilization, birth control methods with post-fertilization mechanisms are considered abortifacient. There is ongoing debate about whether hormonal contraception methods, particularly the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP), have post-fertilization mechanisms. The group Pharmacists for Life has called for a large-scale clinical trial to evaluate EPF in women taking COCPs, which would provide the most conclusive evidence regarding whether COCPs have post-fertilization mechanisms. EPF is also useful in investigating embryo loss prior to implantation. One study in healthy women seeking pregnancy detected 14 pregnancies using EPF, of which six were lost within ten days of ovulation, indicating a 43% rate of early conceptus loss. EPF has been proposed as a tool to distinguish infertility caused by failure to conceive from infertility caused by failure to implant. It has also been suggested as a marker of viable pregnancy, potentially more useful than other chemical markers such as hCG and progesterone in distinguishing ectopic or other nonviable pregnancies. A study of EPF in women taking clomiphene for infertility treatment found fertilization rates of about 40%-50% per cycle. In cycles where fertilization was detected, nearly 80% resulted in subclinical embryonic loss, a much higher rate than in healthy women. A study of EPF in women undergoing in vitro fertilization (IVF) concluded that while many embryos failed to implant, a significant number were likely damaged or killed by the transfer process itself. Researchers used these findings to call for greater attention to the effective transfer of embryos during IVF procedures. Although EPF is almost exclusively associated with pregnancy, EPF-like activity has also been detected in tumors of germ cell origin and other types of tumors. Its utility as a tumor marker, particularly for evaluating the success of surgical treatment, has been suggested.
